data.raw_text:
A dog named Haven has become an internet sensation after miraculously finding his way home two weeks after being swept away by floodwaters during Typhoon Tino in the Philippines.

On November 4, 2025, powerful floods struck Villa del Rio in Barangay Bacayan, Cebu City. Owner Emmanuel Llenos was forced to prioritize rescuing his family and smaller pets, leaving Haven behind in the chaos. Despite extensive searches and appeals on social media, there was no sign of the dog.

The family eventually relocated due to severe flood damage but continued returning to their old home in hopes of a miracle. That miracle arrived when Haven suddenly reappeared — exhausted, covered in mud, but alive. He had found his way back to the exact spot where he was last seen.

Emmanuel described the emotional reunion as overwhelming joy. He also called it “good karma,” recalling how he had rescued a woman stranded on an electric post during the height of the flooding.

data.raw_text:
Rest In Peace.

US Marine Corps Sgt Richard M. Febbi from Butler, NJ.. Rich served in the Marine Corps for four years in Japan, Australia, and Hawaii. He also fought the War on Terrorism in the Philippines. After a short break of service, when he became a Butler Fire Fighter, Rich joined the US Army to become a Calvary Scout.

He was assigned as a Scout Section Leader for the 1st Battalion, 72nd Armed Regimen, located at Camp Casey, Korea. Following his deployment to Korea, Sgt. Febbi was assigned to Ft. Lewis, Washington, Outlaw Troop, 4th Squadron, 2nd Calvary Regiment.

On July 1, 2005, he was tragically killed in a car accident.

One of the suspects was 17 years old, the other was 18. The police are investigating the incident as a hate crime. They declined to give more details.

data.raw_text:
Nephrocare Health Services #HarResultKuchKehtaHai
#FANTASTIC

The headline 108% jump in operating profit reveals a powerful arbitrage play that is still in its early stages. NephroPlus is effectively using its low-cost Indian operational core to service international markets where the revenue per treatment is 3 to 5 times higher. Outside-India revenue now makes up 44% of the total mix, up from 41% just last quarter, which explains why margins expanded by over 800 basis points even as the domestic business faced pricing pressure. Cash quality is the standout feature of this result.

For every ₹100 of reported profit, the company generated over ₹300 in real operating cash this year. This elite conversion has allowed the company to wipe out almost all its debt post-IPO, leaving a ₹283 Cr war chest. You don't see this level of cash generation in traditional hospital models, which typically struggle with high capital intensity and long gestation periods. The next major reveal will be the Saudi Arabia JV. The Riyadh Hospital unit is currently awaiting licensing, and the pricing there is roughly 13 times higher than Indian government reimbursement rates.

Management has already committed ₹70 Cr in collateral for this expansion, and with the first unit expected to start contributing within two quarters, the consolidated revenue per treatment is likely to see another structural leg up. The primary risk remains the opaque regulatory timeline for Saudi licensing, which has historically been lumpy. However, with ₹177 Cr of IPO proceeds still available for clinical expansion and a successful track record of integrating acquisitions in the Philippines, the company appears to have multiple levers to sustain its growth trajectory regardless of any single-market delay.
